tldr: By using a VLM to extract "when and which body parts are critical" from human motions, and concentrating computational resources and interaction weights on these key moments and parts, this framework achieves humanoid object manipulation and reinforcement learning control with high-precision contact at lower computational cost.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed method. (a) Critical body parts and keyframes are identified through a VLM and trajectory analysis, (b) high-fidelity reference trajectories are generated using spatiotemporal preferences and mechanics-aware contact anchoring, and (c) a robust control policy is learned via reinforcement learning with adaptive sampling and contact rewards.
overview:
Motion retargeting, which transfers human whole-body motion data onto humanoid robots, is essential for realizing sophisticated loco-manipulation tasks such as carrying objects while walking. However, humans and robots have substantially different physical structures (embodiments), such as limb lengths and joint ranges of motion. Consequently, existing methods that optimize uniformly across all time frames and body parts not only incur huge computational costs, but also cause hand misalignments at critical stages where contact accuracy is truly vital—such as lifting or placing an object—leading to manipulation failures in both physics simulations and real-world hardware.

To address this issue, this study introduces Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR), a framework that intelligently allocates spatiotemporal preferences. First, by combining a vision-language model (VLM) with trajectory analysis, the system automatically extracts from video "which body parts" play a crucial role and "when" (keyframes). Next, STR allocates a higher iteration budget to these keyframes and assigns higher interaction weights to the participating body parts. Furthermore, Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA) is introduced to refine contact target positions based on object mechanics (force and moment equilibrium).

In simulation experiments on a Unitree G1, the proposed approach reduced the optimization computational cost (SQP iterations) by approximately 76% compared to the prior method (OmniRetarget), while substantially improving geometric contact continuity. Additionally, when training downstream policies with Spatiotemporal Reinforcement Learning (STRL) using these high-quality references, the task success rate dramatically increased from 32.97% to 86.56%. On real Unitree R1 hardware, the robot achieved a 10 out of 10 success rate in box-carrying tasks.
contributions: Proposed a retargeting method (STR) that combines VLM video interpretation with trajectory analysis to automatically detect critical body parts and keyframes in object manipulation, adaptively allocating optimization resources.

Introduced Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA), which estimates the required wrench (force and moment) from object motion and refines stable contact positions while preserving contact surface normal directions.

Developed Spatiotemporal Reinforcement Learning (STRL), which combines adaptive stage sampling based on failure frequencies with contact position rewards to learn high-precision whole-body control policies from retargeted trajectories.
Demonstrated substantial reductions in computational cost and dramatic improvements in task success rate in both Unitree G1 simulation and Unitree R1 real-world experiments.

sections.heading: Why Whole-Body Object Manipulation Needs Spatiotemporal Priorities
sections.summary: When bridging the embodiment gap between humans and robots via retargeting, the success of object manipulation hinges on precision during specific moments and at specific body parts where contacts are formed and maintained. This section points out the inefficiency of uniform per-frame optimization and argues for an approach guided by spatiotemporal preferences.
sections.details:
Human demonstrations are a goldmine for teaching humanoid robots locomotion and whole-body loco-manipulation. However, because humans and robots differ in limb lengths and joint kinematic configurations, joint angles cannot simply be copied directly. The technique that bridges this gap is motion retargeting. In recent years, methods that preserve spatial relationships between meshes (such as OmniRetarget) have improved overall motion fidelity, but conventional techniques lack a clear focus on which moments are most critical and which body parts require the most attention.

In tasks such as picking up and carrying a box, sub-centimeter accuracy between the hands and the object is essential at the moments of touching (Contact) or setting down (Place). During transportation (Carry), whole-body coordination across the hands, arms, and torso becomes the primary factor in supporting the object. A hand misalignment of just a few centimeters at a critical keyframe causes the subsequent grasp and carry to fail completely. Rather than solving every frame uniformly, the system must decide where to focus optimization effort temporally and spatially based on the semantic meaning of the motion.

To tackle this challenge, this paper proposes STR, which uses a VLM to identify keyframes and critical body parts to optimally allocate retargeting resources and weights, MCA to refine contact targets using object mechanics, and STRL to seamlessly connect these reference trajectories to reinforcement learning.

sections.heading: Related Work: Retargeting, Whole-Body Control, and Priority-Guided Learning
sections.summary: This section reviews three areas: motion retargeting, humanoid whole-body control, and priority-guided motion generation. The uniqueness of this research lies in combining geometric constraint optimization with VLM-derived spatiotemporal preferences and physical mechanics models.
sections.details:
### Evolution of Motion Retargeting
Starting from classic inverse kinematics (IK) and spacetime constraints, recent methods have increasingly leveraged neural networks and large-scale body models such as SMPL. In robotics, approaches like GMR (using local scaling) and OmniRetarget (preserving spatial object relations via graph meshes) have emerged. However, because these methods optimize entire trajectories uniformly, they lack a mechanism to selectively concentrate computational effort at critical points such as contacts.

### Humanoid Whole-Body Control and Loco-Manipulation
Reinforcement learning (RL) methods that track reference trajectories (such as DeepMimic, PHC, and HumanPlus) have advanced rapidly. In loco-manipulation involving objects, maintaining contact is exceptionally challenging. While techniques like ResMimic (adding residual policies) and Opt2Skill (imitating trajectory optimization) have been proposed, they face the fundamental bottleneck that training struggles if the underlying reference trajectory possesses poor contact quality.

### Priority- and Importance-Aware Motion Generation
Spatiotemporally, methods such as ExBody prioritize upper-body tracking, while RobotKeyframing and AdaMimic guide trajectories using sparse keyframes. Additionally, utilizing VLMs to extract task geometric constraints (such as ReKep and VoxPoser) has become active. This work distinguishes itself from prior research by recognizing the VLM's strength in high-level semantic understanding and unifying spatiotemporal preferences across retargeting optimization weights, solver iteration budgets, and RL sampling strategies.

sections.heading: STR and STRL: Spatiotemporal Resource Allocation and Mechanics-Aware Anchoring
sections.summary: This section details STR, which identifies keyframes and critical parts via a VLM and trajectory analysis to adaptively allocate SQP iterations and weights. It also presents MCA, which refines contact positions using object mechanics, and STRL, which concentrates reinforcement learning on challenging stages.
sections.details:
### 3.1 & 3.2 Keyframe and Critical Body Part Extraction
The inputs are a human motion video along with estimated SMPL and object trajectories. First, a VLM (Qwen-27B) inspects the video to identify key stages such as "lifting" or "carrying," selecting motion signals suited for detection (such as hand or object velocity) and relevant body parts (hands, pelvis, knees, etc.). Next, the frame-to-frame change rate $\Delta v_t$ of the selected signal is computed, and thresholding determines the keyframe $c_e$ marking the start of each stage.

### 3.3 Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR)
Robot joint trajectories are solved using Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP), with selective resource allocation:
- **Temporal Preference**: An iteration budget of $B_{\text{init}}=50$ is assigned to the initial pose ($t=0$), $B_\tau=4$ to keyframes, and $B_{\text{base}}=2$ to regular frames. While regular frame computation is pruned substantially, solving keyframes with high precision provides strong initializations for subsequent frames. Within each stage, a weight boost factor $\gamma_e(t)$ peaks and decays while maintaining emphasis.
- **Spatial Preference**: Interaction weights $\alpha_{t,i}$ between extracted critical parts (e.g., hands) and adjacent object mesh vertices are scaled up by a factor of 2 to 4.
- **Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA)**: The required wrench $w_t^{\text{req}}$ (force and moment) is estimated from object acceleration during contact. Keeping the contact surface normal direction ($-n_p$) fixed, anchor positions $a_p^\star$ are refined to minimize moment errors. This establishes well-conditioned contact position and orientation tracking objectives ($E_{\text{anchor}}, E_{\text{dir}}$).

### 3.4 Spatiotemporal Reinforcement Learning (STRL)
A whole-body tracking policy is trained using PPO on the resulting high-quality reference trajectories, incorporating two key components:
- **Adaptive Stage Sampling**: Trajectories are segmented into stages, and episode reset points are sampled accordingly. Stages with higher failure rates $f_j$ or higher importance receive higher sampling probabilities, focusing training time on difficult transitions.
- **Contact Position Reward**: A kernel-based reward $r_n^{\text{contact}}$ measures how closely the robot's hands approach and contact the MCA-designed surface anchors, promoting reliable physical grasping in simulation.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Dramatic Computational Savings, Contact Precision, and Real-World Transfer
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted on a simulated Unitree G1 and a real Unitree R1. The approach reduced retargeting computation by approximately 76% while substantially boosting contact continuity, improved RL task success from 32.97% to 86.56%, and achieved a 10/10 success rate in real-world box-carrying tests.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Baselines
Ten diverse human-object interaction tasks involving small tables, plastic boxes, and suitcases were selected from the OMOMO dataset. The simulation used a 29-DoF Unitree G1, while real-world validation was conducted on a Unitree R1 equipped with a Jetson Orin NX. Baselines included PHC, GMR, VideoMimic, and OmniRetarget. Evaluation metrics included Pose Estimated Contact Ratio (PECR), Estimated Contact Continuity (ECC), Foot Skating, SQP iteration count, and RL task Success Rate (SR).

### Retargeting Performance and Computational Cost
As shown in Table 1, the proposed STR achieved exceptional geometric contact metrics. PECR reached 80.19% and ECC reached 72.54%, more than doubling the best prior results (OmniRetarget at 33.65% and 24.63%). Notably, computational efficiency improved dramatically: STR required an average of 353.1 SQP iterations per sequence compared to 1471.1 for OmniRetarget, a reduction of roughly 76%. Qualitative comparisons in Figure 3 show that unnatural gaps between the hands and objects seen in prior methods were eliminated, resulting in tight adhesion to object surfaces.

### Insights from Ablation Studies
Removing spatial preferences (critical part weights and MCA anchors) caused PECR to drop sharply to 34.25%. Removing temporal preferences (keyframe iteration budgets) increased total iterations to 1455.2 while ECC dropped to 68.22%. This demonstrates that allocating more iterations to key moments while pruning regular frames not only saves compute, but is also fundamental to preserving smooth trajectory continuity.

### Downstream RL and Real-World Experiments
In downstream control evaluations (Table 3), using OmniRetarget references with standard RL resulted in a 32.97% success rate, whereas STR references with standard RL jumped to 81.25%. This underscores the decisive impact of reference trajectory contact fidelity. Incorporating STRL (adaptive sampling + contact rewards) pushed the success rate to 86.56%. In real-world Unitree R1 box-carrying experiments (Figure 5, Table 4), the robot completed the task in all 10 trials, demonstrating robust transfer to the physical world.

sections.heading: Appendix: Mechanics-Aware Formulation and Real-World Deployment Setup
sections.summary: This section details the alternating optimization algorithm for force allocation and anchor refinement in MCA, geometric thresholds for contact evaluation, and the real-time control architecture on the Jetson Orin NX deployed on the Unitree R1.
sections.details:
### Detailed Formulation of Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA)
MCA calculates the required wrench $w_t^{\text{req}}$ via inverse dynamics from the object's target linear and angular accelerations. It solves the contact force distribution using quadratic programming under friction cone limits and normal force bounds ($15\,\text{N} \le f_{p}^{\text{n}} \le 40\,\text{N}$). Next, holding forces fixed, anchor positions $a_p$ are shifted within the surface tangent plane to minimize moment errors. Alternating between force distribution and anchor refinement three times yields stable grasp points free of unnatural torques.

### Contact Evaluation Metric Definitions
In PECR and ECC calculations, a geometrically valid contact ($V_{t,k}=1$) is strictly defined when the minimum distance between the contact body and the object collision geometry satisfies $-10\,\text{mm} \le \phi \le 0\,\text{mm}$ (allowing slight interpenetration up to 10 mm) and remains within $10\,\text{mm}$ of the original object surface.

### Hardware Deployment on Unitree R1
Policy inference runs on the robot's onboard Jetson Orin NX (16GB) using Python and ONNX Runtime (CPU execution). The control loop executes policy inference at 50 Hz and low-level PD joint commands at 500 Hz. The task is partitioned into four distinct stages—lifting, standing, walking, and placing—with individually trained ONNX models executed in sequence.

takeaways: Abandoning uniform per-frame optimization in favor of concentrating iterations on critical keyframes cuts computational cost by over 70% while improving trajectory fidelity.
In reinforcement learning for loco-manipulation, the geometric contact accuracy of the reference trajectory itself is the primary bottleneck determining task success, even before reward shaping.
Rather than solving low-level joint control directly, VLMs are highly effective as high-level spatiotemporal attention extractors that identify which parts matter and when.

Aligning contact targets with physical mechanics (wrench equilibrium derived from object motion), rather than relying purely on geometry, directly enhances grasp stability in physical simulation and real hardware.
limitations: Initial contact anchor search relies on heuristics assuming two opposing surfaces (bimanual squeezing grasps), requiring further extension to handle single-arm manipulation or multi-finger contacts.
Object mass and inertia are treated as fixed approximate constants, limiting robustness when physical parameters are unknown or vary significantly.

Real-world deployment explicitly divides tasks into four sequential stages (lift, stand, walk, place) using separate policy models, rather than executing long-horizon tasks via a single end-to-end policy.
